utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, yesterday we have not always assigned numbers to documents that were new which were not already in evidence. I think there are three or four of them. I would like to invite Madam Registrar to just briefly mention them and to assign numbers to them. Madam Registrar. If you need more time for preparation, we'll do it at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think there may be a few more than that, in fact. I think the -- quite a number of the excerpted Assembly -- post-1992 Assembly sessions I think may need a new number as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the whole of the -- of the minutes of those sessions are not in evidence yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Acquaviva had produced a very useful schedule which Madam Registrar could use. She very helpfully distributed it to the parties. It could be done at a later stage, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could do it at a later stage. Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony, and Mr. Tieger is invited to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And in connection with the issues just raised we'll try to liaise with the registrar as well to make sure that all of those items are included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes -- Mr. Krajisnik, you had some maps I think you were talking about yesterday, and I think I invited you to bring them and to give them to the parties so that they can see to what extent they're useful to -- Madam Usher, let's see how many copies we have, and may I have a look at it as well. But they should be distributed to the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had three assignments and I wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so. Let's first, perhaps, look for one second at the maps. I think some of them, but I'm not quite sure. They look all very familiar. I take it that the parties will compare these maps with -- at least map 9 with -- and I'm now talking from my memory, D7 I think it is or -- and compare them and see whether -- see whether it brings any new elements and to see to what extent it's -- would assist the Chamber in receiving them and having them available as evidence. Mr. Krajisnik, this was the one, this was the maps. Second one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These maps were supposed to be our response reflecting that we had accepted deviation from the factual situation; that's the assignment you gave me. And from these maps you can see to what extent we accepted to deviate from the factual situation; that's why I brought this map from 1993, the time of that discussion to which the questions of the Prosecution relate. And second, a statement of mine, an ugly statement about Muslims, was presented here and you gave me the transcript to review it. I found the contribution in which that was mentioned before mind, and I wanted to present this because it really sounded different from what it actually was like and created confusion here. But it would be useful for everyone to take the transcript of the 24th Session dated the 8th of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, please. You said you'd like to draw your attention to a certain portion of the minutes of the tape-recording of the 24th Session. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us begin from my statement, my contribution, 29th page, the last numbers are 934. Let us just look at what I said, and then we will see what it relates to, if you allow me to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, 934 appears to me to correspond to the bottom of page 78 and page 79 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We've got it in front of us, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here: "Here we had a suggestion here. For us to say that it's a religious sect of Turkish orientation because then we would create a rift or that would create a rift in the Muslim world. That means that I picked up somebody else's idea to name it a religious sect." And even further on you can see that I am repeating other people's words and then it goes on. For instance, Saudi Arabia and some other Muslim countries believe that Turks are newly fangled Muslims who eat and drink the same things as others. And let me draw your attention to one more thing. Mr. Kupresanin spoke before me for the second time and he spoke after the conclusions that we had drawn from those deliberations. He also introduced a new topic, namely that Muslims are not a nation, but instead they were Serbs. That was very dangerous because his meaning was that all of Bosnia was Serbian. All the territories taken by Serbs that were formerly Muslims' belonged to Serbs. And I'll tell you exactly the page where somebody else said the same thing. Page 18, and the last numbers are 922. That's the contribution of Kupresanin -- I'm sorry, I gave you the wrong reference. Sorry, it comes a little before that. Page 15, 021149219, Mr. Savo Corda. I'll give you the first -- the last two lines. He says: "We also know that Muslims are no nation. No way. I would always stress in negotiations that they are not a nation. Europe should know that. They are no ethnic community. They are our outcasts on which we cannot agree and we cannot reconcile with it." And then he goes on saying some ugly words that I won't repeat. You can read for yourself. That comes long before the conclusions. It's completely outside the discussion about the Geneva paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Court seems to be following that reference based on the numbers given, but I can't find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to find it. What I see is that Mr. Krajisnik was referring to the B/C/S version. I could follow it to that, but I have not found yet the corresponding pages in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll wait. I'd rather wait. I think it is very useful to read this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's page 60, Your Honour, in the middle of the page: "We also know that Muslims are not a nation. I would always stress that during the negotiations. They are degenerates," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the first reference to what Mr. Savo Corda said might not be -- oh, that's -- yes, I apologise for -- yes. We found it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's line 10, approximately. Let me just tell you that he mentioned it was a creation of the communist party, that we were the oldest nation, et cetera, or one of the oldest nations. 18th page. The last numbers of the ERN number are 922, Kupresanin speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be on page 64 and on from the bottom, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. On this page, it's the second full paragraph when he says: "We didn't need the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." or "the war was not necessary in Bosnia and Herzegovina." 25

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, in fact he's addressing himself to: "We say that the war was not necessary in Bosnia and Herzegovina ..." And then he says: "The war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was necessary ..." And then he continues to explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. That is so. I want to point out that his contribution was completely contrary to the subject under discussion and it was very dangerous. I don't want to bother you with it, but he says that all of it is Serb land, that Muslims were a minority, that a war needs to start in Serbia. I'm trying to go through it as briefly as I can. And then I stress, please go to page 24, the last numbers are 928.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If there's another version of the 23rd Session that's available, we'd be very grateful because I've handed mine now to Mr. Sladojevic in trying to assist and find the place rapidly. If there isn't one, don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's the 24th Session, and let me look very quickly to see if I can assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It looks -- let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a coincidence, but here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very grateful. Page 72 is what Mr. Sladojevic tells me in relation to this last extract.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we found that. Page 72, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am speaking here. Let us just look at one thing in the second paragraph. Since there were misunderstandings a moment ago concerning the press release, let me give just one explanation. During the session of the club of deputies, we intended to make a break and adopt the conclusions which would be adopted at the session in Geneva. I just want to say that there was a club of deputies session that also deliberated about these things. That's why I said there were several references to this. And conclusions are presented here related only to the continuation of the Geneva negotiations, about the Vance-Owen Plan. And when I finished, it's again on page 23 and 24, the last number is 9929, all of it is in the vein that the conference to which most of the MPs were opposed should continue. And now towards the end of the page when we were about to vote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps first I indicated in the B/C/S original we find two pages 24. So the numbering of those pages is a bit confusing. So when you said, Mr. Krajisnik, that you refer to 23 and 24, you are referring to 24, 1, and 24, 2. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. I saw that last night, too. Until page 29. When I was about to present the conclusions for voting, and it was with great effort that we agreed on those conclusions to be put forward at the Geneva Conventions, because everybody was against accepting any kind of talk about the Vance-Owen Plan, Kupresanin comes up again with his insistence that Muslims are not a nation, that all the territories we had taken away from them are Muslim [as interpreted] anyway. So I say: All right. There were all sorts of suggestions. Let us decide whether Muslims are a nation. In fact, the Assembly is not competent to decide whether Muslims are a nation or not, but I didn't want to deny it. I just wanted those conclusions to be ready for the conference. Read here, please. He says that this issue had been discussed at various sessions on many occasions, and it was completely preposterous for the Assembly to decide whether Greeks are Greeks, whether French are French or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Page 78 and 79 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there were two theories. One, that Muslims are Serbs, and the other one that Muslims are not a nation, both of them being dangerous. So at this point I just said: Come on, vote. Are Muslims a nation or not? But those are not originally my words. You will see that all of this had been said at some Assembly session by somebody else or maybe at sessions of the club of deputies. And it was with great effort that we finally adopted those conclusions with which to go to the meeting in Geneva. I reviewed this for the first time. I don't have in my possession any transcripts after 1992. You can see from what I said that I was actually angry about those proposals and about this totally inappropriate theory that we should decide whether Muslims are a nation or not. But it all had to do with maps. It had to be done before the maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you are, as a matter of fact, responding to something that has not been said, and that's not for the first time, therefore I draw your attention to it. No one said that you invented those words; it's only -- your attention is drawn to the fact that you spoke those words, not that you were the first one to speak them. Second, no one has suggested that what you did, that the Assembly was competent to do what it did. I think, Mr. Tieger, that you put questions and you confront Mr. Krajisnik with what the Assembly did. I have not heard any suggestion in your questions that they were competent to do so, so therefore you are at this moment responding to what you consider perhaps dangerous or whatever. But you are more or less engaging in a discussion with an unknown interlocutor who said you invented those words and you spoke them. Only the second portion that you spoke those words, and you did not deny that in your testimony, and now you explain that it was not you who was the first to speak those words or to come up with these ideas. That is, as far as I am concerned - and I'm looking to my colleagues - that is not in evidence. No one ever asked you, no one ever has drawn your attention to you being the one who came up with these ideas or invented them. The only thing that was asked of you, the only thing our attention was drawn to, was that you spoke those words. And, Mr. Tieger, unless I'm mistaken, let's -- let's move on at this moment because you are -- you are entering into --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a debate which, perhaps it's not a clarification only. You are responding to what has not been suggested, until now at least. Of course, if Mr. Tieger comes with any quotation which tend to establish that you are the first one to invent these words, then of course it would be different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, please. It was my understanding yesterday that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine what you've drawn. You've drawn our attention to it at this moment. I'm just telling you that it's important not to have a kind of an internal debate. Yes. One more line and then I'll give Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just say what the assignment was that you gave me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't give you any assignments. You said: I would like to draw your attention to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was my understanding that that is what I had said and that that was my opinion. But it's not my opinion. I said something that somebody else had said, that's the only difference, and it's a big difference, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you repeat the words, Mr. Krajisnik, and if you do not refer to that: This is the opinion of someone else, people might think what you expressed, and if you say, "you're right," that that's your opinion. Because it's difficult to understand otherwise that you're expressing at that moment your opinion about what someone else said. Let's continue now, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger has now an opportunity. I see that we received the B/C/S version of the -- of a statement of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik has provided that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that a different one --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It looks very much as if this is a conversation between Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It's a statement, the one from yesterday, the one that was in dispute, its integral version of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would like it to be admitted into the agenda and could the OTP please give me the statement made by Mr. Filipovic? I would like that to be admitted into agenda -- oh, sorry, not the agenda but the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, we'll have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First we'll leave it to the parties. If the parties think it of any use to have something in evidence, if they think it would assist the Chamber in making its determinations, they'll do so. If, finally, the Chamber would like to see certain documents, then we'll ask for it. Mr. Josse, it's not in evidence. I can't read it anyhow, apart from that it says [B/C/S spoken]. I leave it to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We will investigate that at the next break. Could I just briefly mention the map, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Before it gets --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you finish with that. When I said would you please check whether it's not 7 -- 7 or 7 (B) -- of course, I now notice it is 1993, where 7 and 7 (B) are of 1992, a part of the Cutileiro discussions, whereas it seems that these maps have been introduced as preparing maps for the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think that's right and we have checked very quickly. I'm in Your Honour's hands as to whether Your Honour wants that map from Lord Owen's book to be given a D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll first wait for the parties whether the parties think it of any use to give us details on what happened in 1993. If the parties think it's not important, then of course during the examination of the witness it could be that the Chamber gets interested in receiving that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when we adjourned yesterday we were discussing Dr. Karadzic's speech at the Bosnian Assembly in mid-October 1991. I had suggested to you that -- three things. That Dr. Karadzic was threatening the Muslims with physical extinction, with annihilation, that Mr. Filipovic understood that to be the case, and that finally you were aware that that was what Dr. Karadzic had in mind. We dealt with Mr. Filipovic's view on that yesterday. I'd like to turn this morning to what Dr. Karadzic meant. Now, we have in evidence, Mr. Krajisnik, four intercepted conversations involving Dr. Karadzic during the course of that session which ran from, as I understand it, about 10 October to 15 October. Those are conversations that took place on October 12th, two of them; October 13th; and October 15th. I'm going to draw your attention in particular to one of them, but before I do let me mention three of the others. On October 13th, in a conversation with Momcilo Mandic, that's P64A, P154A, and P92 part, Dr. Karadzic said: "And that is the way Croatia took appeared we know what is going to happen here. That has got nothing to do with Karadzic's or anyone else's decision. We know exactly what is going to happen" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Mandic said: "Definitely, that is clear to people in Belgrade."

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "In just is a couple of days Sarajevo will be gone and there will be 500.000 dead. In one month Muslims will be annihilated in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Number of Serbs will be reduced and Croats will be the only ones to profit because they will keep their municipalities."

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "They asked for it."

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "They, they."

utterances.speaker: MR. MANDIC
utterances.text: "They started all this." On the 12th of October, Dr. Karadzic had a conversation wan unidentified man, that's P64A, P154A. Therefore -- and it's part of what Dr. Karadzic said: "Therefore the Muslims know what it is. It is hell of which 5, 600.000 of them will disappear. I've just spoken to my wife. Our estimation is that there were between 40 and 60.000 dead in the war in Croatia" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- do they have the same numbers I'm just checking. Because you two times referred to 154A. It could well be the case. Let me just find them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be a good thing if I had those documents and if I could look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll first -- or is this a series of -- Mr. Tieger, I am a bit lost as far as the numbers are concerned, but I must admit on my computer I've got only P64A, 154, but A then stands for the -- usually for the transcript and .1 stands for the English translation. And P64A, 154, I've got a conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Vukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have those available in tabs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We can look at the particular item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the Court wishes. The first conversation is found at tab 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And of course we will try to more specifically identify the pre-existing exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, since you promised us more or less yesterday, an index to the later parts of the -- that might assist, but -- if we are now talking about tab 30, if you say it's an unidentified person, is that what you said? At least it was identified by the name of Momo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. I think the second one I mentioned was the unidentified one, Your Honour, from October 12th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first one is -- yes. And the second one we find under tab?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The second one I mentioned with Dr. Karadzic, an unidentified man, is at tab 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tab 29, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And particular references are with respect to the conversation on October 13th found at tab 30 at page 2 of the English, the last -- toward the bottom, approximately the fifth box from the bottom. And in the B/C/S at 03219653 at the top. And the reference at tab 29, the conversation of October 12th between Dr. Karadzic and an unidentified man is found in the English at the third page, approximately the sixth box down. And in the B/C/S at 03219989, approximately the fifth box from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'd like to address Mr. Krajisnik's attention to one more intercept on the same subject and direct him to particular portions of that intercept. That's found at tab 28, a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Gojko Djogo on 12 October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the first reference I'd like to bring your attention to is found at page 3 of the English and 02128923 of the B/C/S, second page of the intercept. Dr. Karadzic says: "Well, he's craze -- they're totally crazy, you know, they". Djogo says: "Where... what's he thinking, to start a war in Sarajevo? Is he crazy?"

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "He's, I think that they, exactly, they should be thrashed if they start a war, they will ... they ... they'll disappear." "There will be rivers of blood." Karadzic: "They will disappear, that people will disappear from the face of the earth if they start now. Our offer was their only chance. Even that was too much, what we offered them, but ..." The next reference which I'd like to bring your attention is found at page 7 of the English and at last four pages 8428 in the B/C/S at approximately the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "No. They don't understand... that the Serbs are at a boiling point, that Serbs are slow to ignite, but that they burn for a long time, they don't have a clue, they ... I can't tell our, I mean, our Muslim partner, for crying out loud, don't you understand that Serbs will fight for their state, not to lose their state, down to the last man." And then he continues about seven boxes down: "They -- they have to know that there are 20.000 armed Serbs around Sarajevo. That's insane. They will -- they will disappear" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found it, 28 -- I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Neither did I, Mr. Tieger, apart from the fact that the transcript says 8428, where we are in the 89 series.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought I read 89, Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know, just to correct. I do not see any reference to the 20.000 there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's my apologies. It's 8927 and in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There we find the 20.000. So you started -- yes. Mr. Krajisnik, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Uh-huh, they have to know there are 20.000 armed Serbs around Sarajevo. That's insane. They will -- they will disappear. Sarajevo will be a karakazan /black cauldron/, where 300.000 Muslims will die. They're not right in the head. I don't know -- now I will have to talk, to talk to them openly. People, don't screw around. There are 3, 400.000 armed Serbs in BiH. What are you thinking of? Plus there's the army and the hardware and everything. Do you think you can just secede like Croatia? And they are literally going. Yesterday they told us that these negotiations of ours between the Assembly session, that a sovereign Bosnia means an independent Bosnia, if Yugoslavia doesn't." And finally the last reference I want to bring your attention to in that intercept it's found at page 9 of the English and page 8928 of the B/C/S, just slightly lower than the middle of the page. It's the -- it's that portion, Mr. Krajisnik, where Dr. Karadzic speaks and immediately afterwards Djogo says: "Da, znam."

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC SPEAKING
utterances.text: "We will not force them to do anything but they don't have a way to carry out a secession. I think that this is clear to the army and clear to everyone. It will be a real bloodbath. This time the army won't use only two planes anymore of the 500 it has. It will use 20 for each assault and that would be it then. If Bosnia goes up in flames, Sandzak will follow and Kosovo, you know." Djogo: "Yes, I know."

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "No, there will no longer be." Djogo: "No, no." Karadzic: "He's talking about with Europe." Djogo: "It will be terrible." Karadzic: "Europe will be told to go fuck itself, not to come back until the job is finished." And perhaps one more, with the Court's permission. At the middle of page 8 in the English and the -- 8927 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC SAYS
utterances.text: "We're not banning them from establishing certain," "certain," it looks like. Djogo: "And then in the end they'll enter Banja Luka" -- And then Karadzic says: "Yes, to Ozren, to Doboj, anything. He can rule over half of Sarajevo, Zenica, and half of Tuzla and that's it. It's finished. Gracanica and the small -- but he -- they don't understand that they'd be up to their in their necks in blood and that the Muslim people would disappear. The poor Muslims would disappear who don't know where he's taking them, or at least taking the Muslims." Mr. Krajisnik, do you dispute that Dr. Karadzic, in addressing -- in making his address at the Bosnian Assembly in mid-October 1991 was warning the Muslim people or threatening the Muslim people that if they move forward on plans for independence, that they would face physically annihilation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic was rightly cautioning the Muslim people. The words are too strong. Now, whether they can constitute a threat is something that only the Muslims can feel. I understood this to be a cautioning and a plea for them to give up on independence. You're right. The emphasis was that the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina in an unconstitutional way can lead to grave consequences, and he used these words that the Muslims can disappear. Not biologically, I don't know, but that's the way he spoke, meaning that as a people, as a nation -- well, psychologically they will be broken. I cannot interpret the psychology either of the Muslims or of Mr. Karadzic. I can just tell you how I took this speech. I am confirming to you that, yes, this was a warning that was strongly worded and that had to do with the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina in an unconstitutional way. But there is a correction here. Maybe you didn't notice. Sorry about that. You said here 02 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter could not catch the number; it was too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Karadzic says: "We do not prevent them from setting up detachment," "odred," but it's not "odred," it's "odredje," which would be "odredjene," except if the word was not fully printed out, it would be "odredjene," which is certain something, a certain this, a certain that. "Odredj" is a military formation, detachment, but the word he actually wanted to use here was "odredjene."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the page number because the interpreters could not hear it. The last three digits of the B/C/S would do, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 8927, where Radovan Karadzic is speaking, as quoted by the Prosecutor. That is one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, box number eleven. "We, we are not preventing them from setting up 'odredj' ..." I assume he was saying "odredjene teritorijas," certain territories, it couldn't be "odred," detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's not of vital importance at this moment, although it's a detail, Mr. Josse. If there's any reason to revisit this matter, then we'll hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you were aware before Dr. Karadzic made this speech that he believed that the threat of devastating -- well, the threat of Serb action in response to Muslim moves forward independence was something he was contemplating telling the Muslims? In other words, as a way of deterring the Muslims from moving forward toward independence, Dr. Karadzic was considering saying to them essentially what he said on October -- in mid-October 1991 and what he said to the interlocutors in his telephone conversations around the same time.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he talked to me and he used that word. And I said to him: You shouldn't say the Muslims are going to be annihilated. Everybody's going to be annihilated, we'll all be annihilated, exactly, in this telephone conversation. You can find that telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Actually, the telephone conversation's in front of you if you need to look at it. But let me just ask you a question or two about what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know my own conversation, that's why I'm saying he said that to me in one telephone conversation: They will disappear. And I said don't say they will disappear, we'll all disappear. It was in this one particular telephone conversation. But I did not think that he would speak this way at the Assembly meeting. I can tell you why I think he spoke this way, in case you're interested. I think it was wrong. He shouldn't have put it this way. I agree, and I think that he himself repented that -- about that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I had thought you already told us what you knew about that -- about Dr. Karadzic's remarks in the mid-October Assembly during the course of your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no -- well, perhaps I didn't say it, but it would be very useful to you. Only 15 days before that, at this same Assembly, we reached a conclusion that no one will impose any solutions on anyone, and Mr. Karadzic was terribly angry one all of a sudden they wanted to impose a solution in an unconstitutional way. I understood his statement as a warning, but it was not a good thing at the time, and certainly it was not exactly well measured and he shouldn't have spoken that way. That's what I think. I think if somebody asked him about it now, if he's to be honest about it, that is what he'd say. But that's it, any other people, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't focussing on the extent to which Dr. Karadzic's remarks were well measured, but let's be plain about this. Dr. Karadzic was upset and angry about what he considered to be continuing moves by the Muslims toward independence, and he told them in no uncertain terms: You continue to do this and you face annihilation at the hands of the Serbs. That's it in a nutshell, isn't it? Whether it was well measured or not.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's the point, with all due respect, Mr. Prosecutor. He was scared and angry, and he used big words, totally baseless as they were, but he didn't speak about annihilation, as I understood it. It was not a good statement, like many other statements were not good. But we had reached an agreement with the other side before that, and when that agreement fell through, then he said what he said in resignation using words like: You will disappear, et cetera. At that session, the commission had worked five days to develop that agreement, the agreement was accepted and then fell through. I'm just telling you my impressions with the best intention of telling the truth, and of course everyone is free to interpret what they read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, this brings me to a point of course everyone is free to interpret matters as they want. I mean, we now for quite some time are now discussing what interpretation should be given to certain words. And to be honest, to go into a long debate again and again, it's clear now that Mr. Krajisnik often takes a more favourable interpretation, more favourable in terms of whether there were any bad intentions, yes or no, and it doesn't come as a surprise that the Prosecution interprets these speeches differently. To use too much time on that -- of course, it's good to establish that Mr. Krajisnik had a different interpretation, saying he didn't use the words "annihilation," but it's also clear that there's also a lot of words about bloodshed, et cetera, and if Mr. Krajisnik says: Of course this is not about biological annihilation, then I don't know how to interpret "blood" anything else than in biological terms. Of course you can say it's exaggerated and no one will, I think, deny that emotions go higher and higher people are now using words which they would not have used if they were less emotional at that time. But so -- it's only of limited use to do this exercise for all of the sessions we still have in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's not my intention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I may say, with respect. First of all, I take the Court's words to mind, of course, and it's not surprising, as the Court noted, that in many instances I can anticipate Mr. Krajisnik's -- the interpretation that he will offer. But what can also be relevant, of course, is the interpretation that is offered in the context of the events at the time and in the face of all evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in some instances the Prosecution seeks to do that. I fully accept the Court's guideline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me give you a one-liner. I hate to do it, but a lengthy discussion on whether it was a warning or a threat is not something that really assists the Chamber. We have one very factual question on tab 30. Mr. Krajisnik, you were -- it was put to you that there was a conversation between Mr. Karadzic and Momo on the 13th of October, 1991. That is a Momo who seems to have just returned from Belgrade, where he wanted to visit his son; a Momo who says that he went to Han Pijesak on Friday and that he had a meeting with the armies, the federal SUP, Gracanin was there. Is that you or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not me, it's Mandic. There was Mandic, Zepinic, Delimustafic there, and the others. It's the MUP of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Delimustafic and Zepinic were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So this conversation at tab 30, Momo is Mandic and not you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I make my comment, I'll indicate to the Court I'm moving on from that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But just to make it clear and I'm sorry if there was any ambiguity about that. This is not a debate or was not a -- the point was not focussed on any distinction between warning or threat, which I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. I just gave it as an example of how, while interpreting, you can spend a lot of words on matters that -- that would not really clarify much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree and that certainly wasn't intended to be the focus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, at the risk of one-liners.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honour, just add something in relation to this question? I am not Mr. Karadzic's lawyer, and I don't want to defend him, and it's not my job. I just want to say that we had the entire text of his statement where he says: "Please, I'm warning you." That's how I understood it. I'm not saying he didn't say the Muslim people wouldn't disappear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the only thing you're now doing is to continue what I just explained as being not very useful and not very helpful. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, during the course of your -- during the course of your examination-in-chief you were asked about, among other things, the 18 October 1991 meeting of the Deputies' Club at which Dr. Karadzic advised the assembled members that a team made up of the leading men of the party, the government, and the Political Council has been working day and night. "I have decided to impose a state of emergency in the party. Please inform the others that the party is working in emergency conditions." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, that state of emergency that Dr. Karadzic announced he would impose three days after the remarks to which we've just directed our attention was, in fact, imposed and the cadres of the SDS were duly alerted. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've explained this already in one of my responses, but I can repeat. Specifically, it was Novi Travnik, Zepce, and some other places where the state of emergency was introduced, but it boiled down only to duty service, as far as I know. And Mr. Karadzic said what he said in response to Mr. Djokanovic, who said that we should go to war. He said it to calm the tempers of the audience who heard that. That's what I said previously. You can check it on the transcript. There's a response from Novi Travnik and the SDS describing what they had done in response to his call, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, first of all, Mr. -- well, let me develop that a little further. First of all, at the time of the Assembly session at which -- which we've been speaking about, as a general matter the party was in a state of alert and people were calling in to find out if there were new instructions arising from the situation. That's generally true, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All personnel of Serb ethnicity, whether members of the SDS or not, were anxious to know what they should do because the memorandum and the platform that had been adopted illegally were a terrible shock to the Serbs. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And like Mr. Tintor, found at tab 37 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I think we'll need a number for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't it be better, Your Honour, to do that after the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could do that and then have a chronological order rather than anything else. Madam Registrar, you're invited to include this on the list you are preparing for assigning exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the first page on the English at the bottom and the second page of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, you'll see the portion to which I want to direct your attention. This is Mr. Tintor calling the SDS party asking first for doctor -- for the doctor, who's not in, and then indicating at the portion I just indicated: "Fine. All right. I just want to see if there are any new instructions. So nothing then." So like Mr. Tintor in this intercept, it's correct that not only people were, as a general matter, anxious to know what they should do because the memorandum and platform, according to you, had been illegally adopted but were calling in to the party to find out what steps, if any, should be taken at that point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not witness that, but I can confirm that the entire infrastructure on the Serb side was there, members and nonmembers discussing what to do because it was a dangerous moment that Serbs were frightened of. It was not a simple, regular step, the memorandum and the platform, it was completely unconstitutional, and that has been proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then Dr. Karadzic prepared and had disseminated the state of emergency. If you'll turn to page 40 -- tab 40, excuse me. And on the first page beginning slightly below the middle in the English and further toward the bottom in your version, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Karadzic, after saying earlier: "Put it like this: Send to all the committees, the municipal committees," states or begins to apparently dictate or direct the text of this. "In view of the statutory authorisation, I hereby declare the state of emergency." A few lines down: "I hereby declare the state of emergency of the SDS." And then continues on to the -- in the middle of the second page in English and the second page of your version at about -- for you, Mr. Krajisnik, about three-quarters of the way down: "Besides other measures, you will be informed about the measures of the state of emergency on a daily basis. And the first measure is," and Miljana says: "Go on." "Permanent sessions, everyday sessions, everyday sessions of municipal committees and 24 hours a day, duty hours." Mr. Krajisnik, you have no reason to assert, do you, that that was not -- that Dr. Karadzic had said anything other in this conversation than to ensure that the state of emergency was prepared and made known to all SDS municipal committees?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He practically informed everybody that he had introduced the state of emergency, specifying what it consists of. So you're right. He dictated this paper that was to be sent to all boards, all committees, introducing state of emergency, round-the-clock duty service, and indicating that other instructions would follow. Whether, indeed, any instructions followed, I don't know, but you're right. He specified hear what the state of emergency consists of. And one more thing. State of emergency, because of what happened, not because of what was about to happen, not because the Assembly would be proclaimed but because of what happened on the 14th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the benefit of the registrar, this is an intercept of -- the mentioned item was an intercept of October 17th, 1991, between Dr. Karadzic and Miljana. That's found at tab 40 and we'll need a number as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be added to the list Madam Registrar is preparing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And turning quickly to tab 45, Mr. Krajisnik, this is a conversation of 19 October 1991, between Jovan Tintor and Mr. Krunic. And at the fourth page of the English at the bottom, and the last page of your version, Mr. Krajisnik, in B/C/S, Mr. Tintor states: "Well, we need to -- the situation is now -- I can tell you it's -- the state of emergency is declared, you know, in the party also and all that." Krunic: "Yes, I know, this guy told me yesterday."

utterances.speaker: MR. TINTOR
utterances.text: "Yes, we should work on regionalisation with the" -- And Krunic says: "Yes, sure." First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, that's a reflection of the dissemination of the state of emergency beyond the two municipalities you mentioned earlier - correct - that you mentioned Zavidovici and Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I said that this was an example of responses from those two municipalities as to how they understood the state of emergency. They introduced round-the-clock duty service and they were waiting further instructions, but here I see what Mr. Karadzic had dictated and it's certain that everybody received it -- or maybe somebody didn't receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in terms of what the municipalities understood, by way of the declaration of the state of emergency was, as noted by Mr. Tintor, that regionalisation should be intensified or moved forward, among other things?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assure you, I guarantee, that everybody at the level of municipality understood this as they pleased, as it suited them. And everybody interpreted this instruction from Mr. Karadzic according to their specific situation. The instructions were not even necessary, if you take into account how shocked people were by what happened on the 14th. I know that the surprise of the people was enormous and it was a great problem. Every municipality did whatever they thought best. People were scared out of their wits.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in terms of the information and instructions being disseminated from the top levels of the SDS to the cadres below, you had an opportunity to discuss during the course of your examination-in-chief the 26th October Sarajevo SDS order. You looked at the during the course of your examination, but it is found at tab 49, if we need to look at it. And if I understood you correctly you suggested that it might have been Mr. Brdjanin extrapolating from or expanding on what Dr. Karadzic had said at a meeting, rather than reflecting the position of the SDS leadership and the actions that Dr. Karadzic wanted to see taken?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. That's what I thought. I don't know what they were saying, but I assumed that he expanded. There are lots of illogical things said here that were not eventually done, and they were absolutely not appropriate to the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There was a speech given by Dr. Karadzic in November of 1991 concerning the plebiscite. That's found at tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have tab 3, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Could that be provided back to Mr. Krajisnik then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because I took some things back yesterday, and I am afraid I've left them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me quickly bring your attention to a couple of the things Dr. Karadzic said and ask if you recall that speech. At page 6 of the English and page 00270634 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik, Dr. Karadzic says: "I'm telling you whatever Bosnia we have one day, no Muslim foundation shall ever be laid in Serb areas and Serb villages whether or not you import Turks because we will instruct Serbs not to sell land to Muslims." He goes on to address that issue further down the page.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you tell me at which line I can find that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe you can find the portion I just read to you at --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. That portion actually begins at the bottom of page 0633.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And continuing on to the next page of your version but the same page in English, page 6. "The world will understand when we tell them that we will not allow the demographic picture to change, either naturally or artificially. No way. Our territories are ours. We may be hungry, but we will be there," and then he continues a couple of sentences later. "You must not sell land to Muslims, you must not, because this is a fight to the finish, a battle for living space." First of all, my question first, Mr. Krajisnik, is if you recall your presence at this speech of Dr. Karadzic in Sarajevo shortly before the plebiscite. And I can indicate that your name and Mrs. Plavsic and other Bosnian Serb leaders are mentioned throughout the speech.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended also one meeting discussing how to preserve the country. I don't remember attending this might, but I can respond to your question regarding these words of Mr. Karadzic. I am familiar with this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not directing my -- the reason I brought that to your attention is to see if you have any specific recollection of your attendance at this -- during the course of this fairly lengthy speech of Dr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't know whether my learned friend has any idea where this speech was delivered. That might help the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I indicated Sarajevo. That's as specific as I can be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I asked you that, Mr. Krajisnik, because if you'll look to the last -- latter portion of the speech at page 9 of the English and page 0637 of your version --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found the page. Could you just tell me which line it is, if that's not a problem, because it's barely legible here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You'll want to look to the -- what would roughly be the beginning of the last third of that page and see the name "Brdjanin" mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In one place I see: "Everything that Brdjanin wrote," is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: DR. KARADZIC SAYS
utterances.text: "You -- you, presidents of municipalities, you have to do this job. You and especially if the army instructs you to do it, no one else, no official. You and no one else. Because you are presidents of the National Defence Councils and you are commanders of your towns. And also in Krajina, especially where the war is going on, everything that Brdjanin has written for you. Usually there are forgeries but this is not a forgery. All that Brdjanin wrote to you, apply everything. We are at war. They are attacked us. We are at war." So there Dr. Karadzic is making clear that the -- well, first of all, do you have any doubt that what Dr. Karadzic is referring to in connection with what Brdjanin wrote to you is the 26 October Sarajevo SDS order that Brdjanin signed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time -- well, I mean, if I were listening to these words now I wouldn't know what Brdjanin wrote and I could not react. And I don't know whether that's it or whether it's something different. But I can put this together, what you showed a few minutes ago and what Brdjanin signed is probably what this refers to. But even now if I were to look at it and if I were to hear it, I couldn't say when I didn't attend a meeting. It would be hard for me to interpret why some things were referred to there, when in fact the war was still far away from us. He is saying here: We are at war, but he is referring to Western Slavonia; that's Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And he's urging all the assembled people, and especially the presidents of municipalities, to implement what Brdjanin has provided to them. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can see, that's what's written here, but I really don't know whether it pertains to that or something else. It was probably this, but I don't know. I didn't know about this Brdjanin document then, so I couldn't say. But I saw it when I came here, to The Hague Tribunal or, rather, The Hague prison. And when I reacted to this thing by Brdjanin, I hadn't read this, so I could not realise why it was written the way it was. And that is why I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock. At the same time, Mr. Krajisnik, the question was quite clear and simple: Was he referring to the document we just saw. Your answer is also quite simple: I don't know because I had no knowledge at that time of that document. Then the next line, from what I understand should have been: If I would make an inference, and then it's clear to us already that there are no facts, that you find it probable that the reference was to that document. Three, four lines, that's all, and we spent ages on it. Mr. Tieger, you're also invited to perhaps put questions in such a way that we get the short answers. It's also a matter of technique of questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you are absolutely right, and you know how hard it is when you sit here and you get carried away. I'm so sorry. I tried to explain something. I wished for you never to be in a position to sit here and to try and explain things. I'm so sorry. I'm trying to be of assistance; it's not that I'm trying to get things even more complicated. I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not blaming anyone; I'm encouraging to have this examination --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- more efficient. We stand adjourned until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to turn next to the 3rd Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, which you discussed at length with Mr. Stewart during the course of your examination-in-chief. That was the -- that was held on December 11th, 1991, and as you described in your examination-in-chief, that was the session at which there was discussion about both the establishment of ...

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the 11th of December. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I was indicating, that's the session that you discussed in some detail earlier at which there was discussion about both the establishment of Serbian Municipal Assemblies in Serb minority municipalities and discussion by various deputies about regionalisation. You recall that, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall this session. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you had a -- you answered some questions by His Honour Judge Hanoteau about what the deputies were proposing and what was radical about it, and you described the distinction between the establishment of Serbian municipalities in Serb minority -- Serbian Assemblies in Serb minority municipalities and regionalisation. The -- and in addition, your counsel pointed you to and you described various portions of the Assembly session when the discussion turned to the proposal to establish Serb Assemblies in those minority municipalities and when the discussion turned to regionalisation. Your position was that you advocated the establishment of Serb Assemblies in Serb minority municipalities in contrast to and in opposition to the radical efforts by some of the deputies to promote and further regionalisation. Is that essentially it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of what you said is right. Just a small correction, please. The item on the agenda was the decision on establishing Municipal Assemblies in areas where Serbs were a minority, and then the question of regionalisation was inserted by different people into that same item and that was a completely different issue. It was not radical, it was something that was quite different from the item that was actually on the agenda. But it is true that some people did advocate regionalisation. You're right, yes. And they were challenging this decision. They didn't want to accept this decision on the establishment. First there was this decision, and then there was a recommendation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, were you for or against the -- what you described as the radical attempts by the deputies to advance regionalisation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my opinion was that we were talking about an item on the agenda that had to do with this recommendation to establish municipalities where Serbs were a minority. And now if you're asking me if I was in favour of regionalisation as a political response at that point in time, yes, I was in favour of that, because that was a response to the unconstitutional conduct of this - what do you call it? - the Muslim side. So as a political response, yes, but that was not the item that was actually on the agenda. And I can just remind you of one more thing. On the 25th of January --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, no, no --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in fact during the course of that discussion various people assured those who were talking about advancing regionalisation during the course of the discussion on the establishment of Serb Assemblies, that those two things in fact complemented each other and were not in complicate. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some people were saying that but I don't think they persuaded anyone but later on we passed a decision or a recommendation to establish municipalities because people were confusing the establishment of municipalities with establishment of Assemblies and these are two different matters all together. When you establish a municipality, that's regionalisation, but when you establish an Assembly, that is not regionalisation. So territory, that's a municipality, and the Municipal Assembly is a body. And the recommendation is to establish Municipal Assemblies. That is what I said then by way of distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. The distinction you're drawing is fully understood, Mr. Krajisnik. What I also want to be understood is that you were assuring the deputies that there was no conflict between the two and that the establishment of Serb Assemblies in minority municipalities was not in any way in conflict with regionalisation, which would continue.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it does not impede regionalisation in any way; you're quite right. The establishment of Serb municipalities where Serbs were a minority does not impede the continuation of regionalisation if we opt for regionalisation because these are two different notions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So you weren't upset with any of the deputies were promoting the idea of regionalisation; you just wanted everything to be done in the particular order of the agenda and you wanted everything focussed on one item at a time. That's basically it.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to work on the basis of the agenda. You're right on that. To discuss this decision which later turned into a recommendation to establish Municipal Assemblies where Serbs were minority, not to mix apples and pears, not to mix regionalisation with that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in fact, regionalisation was underway and was being pursued at the time of that Assembly. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the record you will see that it was not underway and that the main argument of the opponents of this recommendation was that we hadn't even completed regionalisation and that it's not functioning and that we're doing that, we should be doing that now, not to give recommendations to establish Municipal Assemblies. That's what it says in the minutes. It was there on paper and there were attempts, too, but it did not actually operate in the field except in the Krajina up to a point. That is in these minutes. Mr. Kasagic said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The SAOs, the autonomous regions, had been verified at the 2nd Assembly Session on November 21st, 1991. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right. That's right, yes. Yes. It was only then that they had been verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And although, as you indicated, there were people who were dissatisfied with the progress of regionalisation, there were those who had been more active and more successful. For example, at page 15 of the English of this session and page SA024952.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was one of the occasions on which you were trying to clarify for the deputies that you wanted to deal with these issues one at a time. And you said: "Only municipalities where Serbian delegates are a minority should form Assemblies, as this republic Assembly of ours is, so as to exercise certain rights. I think this is the source of the misunderstanding. Veselinovic spoke about regionalisation, the rounding-off of territories, like Mr. Vjestica and others are doing." And that was a reflection of your understanding that Mr. Vjestica in Bosanska Krupa had been making more progress than some of the others?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position here was, as far as what Vjestica was saying is concerned - now whether he actually did this or not, I don't know - but I was trying to explain to Veselinovic that that was what regionalisation was. I was trying to say before this session on the 21st that in fact he carried out some referendum and reached decisions on the annexation of the regionalisation. Annexation is something different from regionalisation. So I took this example and wanted to explain it to Veselinovic who wanted regionalisation, he didn't want the recommendation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Another example of that annexation could be found in the comments of Mr. Kupresanin at page 26 of the English and page 39 of the B/C/S. And I think -- who said the following: "In Bosanska Krajina we have the following situation. We have vast territories, special in Prijedor where over 70 per cent, even up to 80 per cent is Serb territory. The plebiscite has shown us accurately which territory is ours and in accordance with the plebiscite we have to annex this territory. The situation is similar in Bosanska Krupa also, where there are few Serb inhabitants, but about 80 per cent of the territories belong to the Serbs. We must include that territory, too, and form a Serb municipality." And that's a similar example, Mr. Krajisnik, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's talking about municipalities, to establish Serb municipalities, not Assemblies. Well, I can say that Mr. Kupresanin invited Bihac, Cazin, and everybody else to join them in the Krajina. There was this article about that. He wanted to have the entire Krajina to be complete, and that includes Muslim municipalities, and I can document that for you if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I hadn't mentioned previously that the formatting of the cover page sometimes created a problem. I didn't know if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's always minus one, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in fact, Mr. Miskin, at that same session, gave a lengthy address about regionalisation. And I think you'll find that at page 30 of the English and page 024980 of the B/C/S, SA024980. It begins, continuing for quite a while --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, now you are adapted to the new system because minus one gives us a problem, though. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. That may have been one of the instances where they are actually not precisely one page off, or, you're right, I may have adapted earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And at page 36 of the English -- excuse me. Page 32 of the English and SA024983, Mr. Miskin indicates after a discussion of what Bosnia and Herzegovina would look like if it stayed within Yugoslavia notes that: "If Bosnia and Herzegovina divided into regions and if it were to cease to exist as a single republic, then the autonomous regions would comprise the territory of the republic." And he finally ends after his lengthy description of how regionalisation was progressing and its purpose at page 36 of the English and SA02 --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 51? 51, towards the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, if you -- oh, you're looking at the particular pages. I'm referring you to --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, the interpreter was wondering.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: SA024988 and at page 36 of the English Mr. Miskin indicates, following his address: "The principle is known, so there you are, gentlemen, get to work." And that was both the efforts undertaken by Mr. Miskin to prepare his address, the presentation of his remarks to the Assembly, and his concluding comments were a reflection of the ongoing role of regionalisation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is a report of the commissions. That's a second item on the agenda, and he was president of this commission that dealt with regionalisation. So this is the second item on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, at the same page Mr. Miskin made the following remarks. And it's page 36 of the English, as I have it here, and for you, Mr. Krajisnik, found at SA024989. "Given the conditions of war in the country and the very precarious situation in BiH, we believe that in all the regions and in the entire BH detailed contingency plans should be elaborated in the event the Serbian people has to defend itself against various enemies." Now, in fact, Mr. Krajisnik, such detailed contingency plans and preparations were prepared, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this plan except for what Mr. Kapetina testified here, if that's the same thing, but I'm not aware of that plan. This is a report of Mr. Miskin as to what should be done in December 1991. Maybe a plan was proposed, but I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps this is a good time to talk about the Variant A and B document which you testified about on the sixth day of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be good to have this document before me, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to ask you about the details of the document, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At least not at this moment. But I do recall that you indicated a general lack of familiarity with the document, suggested that the document was not important in any way, and noted in particular with respect to Mr. Cizmovic's explicit reference to the instructions at the 6th Session on January 26th that you "simply didn't note [Realtime transcript read in error "know"] it" because you were focussed on the main topic of that day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you help me. The tenth day of Mr. Krajisnik's testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The sixth day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The sixth day, then I understood it wrongly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I ask my learned friend to repeat the words in inverted commas.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, "simply didn't note it."

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, n-o-t-e.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was mistranscribed, and is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The transcript now reads "know" where the words were "note."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I thought it might be helpful, Mr. Krajisnik, to actually focus the Chamber on the backdrop to the succession and to Mr. Cizmovic's involvement in events up to time as well as your own and the events that followed. Now, we've heard considerable testimony, of course, about the A and B document, and in particular its distribution around the time of the 4th Bosnian Serb Assembly Session on the 21st of December, 1992. You also testified about that session and events that occurred during the course of that session. That was a session at which the Council of Ministers was established, the individuals ministers were selected and the ministerial council itself was established. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the ministers were not selected. The ministerial council was formed instead from the ministers on the government Bosnia and Herzegovina, just as Serb assemblies were formed for Serb assemblymen in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And if you want to know about Cizmovic, I can give you a separate response about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'll be asking you specific questions so there won't be any confusion about what I want to know about. In terms of the selection of persons for the ministerial council, it wasn't simply the case, was it, that persons who were -- who occupied a ministerial or a specific ministerial post in the joint government became -- took an equivalent position in the Bosnian Serb Council of Ministers. There was also some concern about Mr. Zepinic expressed and you resolved that concern yourself by proposing that Mr. Stanisic become a minister without a portfolio on the Council of Ministers. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I can give an explanation in response to your question whether they held any positions or not. I don't remember having explained about Zepinic. Maybe I did. If it's written there, then I probably did, and I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I was simply focussing, Mr. Krajisnik, on your suggestion that the ministerial council was established exclusively by the existing positions occupied by those individuals in the joint government. I appreciate that that was generally how it worked, but I wanted to point out at least this exception and that the establishment of the ministerial council at least had some discretionary element. That's fair. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were more and I can explain; however, my first answer is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But maybe you want to know why my first answer is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your first answer being that for the -- that -- being that persons who occupied a ministerial post in the joint government became members of the Bosnian Serb Council of Ministers in an equivalent position. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would not be a complete answer. Maybe I said that, but in fact Serb personnel in certain ministries, maybe they were not ministers, maybe they were assistant ministers or clerks at the ministry, in any case that person was included in the ministerial council. Those were Serb personnel in the ministries, not necessarily all ministers. And they were all taken into the ministerial council, and I can explain about Zepinic in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I appreciate that clarification. And I think, as you noted, the discussion that took place in the Assembly addressed that issue or reflects that issue.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It was as item number 2 or maybe 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And in addition, the Council of Ministers included a coordinator for the autonomous regions, Mr. Cizmovic, and he was selected as a member of the Council of Ministers in that post. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was elected coordinator either of the ministerial council or coordinator of autonomous regions. We can check that in the papers. I think he was coordinator of autonomous regions. Anyway, it was a coordinating position. He may have been on the ministerial council, but I think he was coordinator of autonomous regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll look quickly at page 34 and 35 of the English and --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry to give you so much trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you'll find that at SA025131 through 5133 of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. Yes, I found it, if that's Jovo Mijatovic about the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And he's reciting the decision on the appointment of coordinators of activities of the executive bodies of the Serbian autonomous regions and the Autonomous Region of Krajina on the -- at the bottom of page 34 --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 34, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
